headline: Microsoft 365 Family shares Copilot AI benefits with up to 5 others
summary: Previously limited to the primary account holder, AI features are now shareable across Microsoft 365 Family and Premium plans. However, OneDrive storage is consolidated to a shared 2TB pool.
details: Microsoft is rolling out the ability for Microsoft 365 Family and Premium subscribers to share Copilot and other AI-powered features with up to five additional users. This expands access beyond the primary account holder, who was the sole beneficiary of these AI tools since their bundling last year.

The update aims to provide more flexible AI usage for families and premium subscribers. This change comes a year after the launch of Microsoft 365 Premium, which combines Copilot Pro and Microsoft 365 Family benefits for $19.99 per month.

A significant change accompanying this feature expansion is the consolidation of OneDrive storage. Instead of each user receiving 1TB, all members on a Microsoft 365 Family plan will now share a total of 2TB of OneDrive storage. Microsoft states this offers greater flexibility if one member exceeds their individual limit, though it could also encourage users to purchase additional storage.

Microsoft has acknowledged the storage shift and mentioned that existing subscribers in eligible markets may receive transitional bonus storage. The company also plans to offer support for families experiencing high storage usage, indicating awareness of potential user concerns regarding the reduced individual storage allocation.

headline: Quake ported to safe Rust and playable in the browser
summary: Experience the 1996 classic with software rendering directly in your web browser, no GPU required. The shareware episode is included.
details: A developer has successfully ported the original Quake to Rust, a modern systems programming language known for its safety features. This new version allows the classic first-person shooter to be played directly within a web browser.

The port utilizes software rendering, meaning it does not require a dedicated GPU, making it accessible on a wider range of devices. Players can add their own Quake game files to experience all four episodes.

The project is open-source and available on GitHub, with the original shareware episode included for immediate play. This initiative brings a piece of gaming history to the web in a new, accessible format.
Quake, originally released by id Software in 1996, was a groundbreaking title that popularized 3D graphics and multiplayer gaming. This Rust port aims to preserve and share that legacy.
